title: Stone tools found beneath Australia's drowned coast
dek: Archaeologists have identified submerged stone artefacts linked to a freshwater spring and a rocky hill in north-western Australia, revealing how Aboriginal communities used landscapes now under the sea.
body: The discoveries were made in the Murujuga region of Western Australia, where researchers found stone artefacts associated with an ancient freshwater spring and a rocky hill overlooking a former river channel. These sites were submerged at least 9,000 years ago following rising sea levels after the last Ice Age. The findings suggest the artefacts could be considerably older than the inundation date. The study was published in Quaternary Science Reviews by archaeologists from Flinders University, the University of Western Australia, James Cook University and the University of York, working with the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation.

One site is tied to a freshwater spring, which would have been a vital resource for people living in the area before it was flooded. The second site is located near a rocky hill that once overlooked an ancient river channel, showing how different landscape features were used. Together, they indicate these are not isolated finds but part of a wider cultural landscape that existed when the continental shelf was dry land.

Analysis of the stone tools shows some were made from raw materials sourced near Rosemary Island, about 23 kilometres from where they were found. This implies the deliberate selection and transport of stone across a landscape now beneath the seabed. Such movement suggests planning and knowledge of distant resources, indicating complex behaviour by ancient communities.

The research involved Murujuga Rangers Malik Churnside and Richard Variakojis, who received scientific diving training and took part in underwater surveys. Their direct involvement highlights the role of Indigenous knowledge in identifying and documenting the submerged sites. Vincent Adams of the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation said the work shows the cultural landscape extends far beyond today’s coastline into Sea Country.

Professor Jonathan Benjamin, lead author from Flinders University, said the collaboration demonstrates the value of working with trained Indigenous Rangers who contributed to the challenging research. He noted that flooded landscapes did not simply disappear but remain part of Country, preserving evidence of people’s lives and connection to place. Each discovery adds a chapter to Australia’s deep human story.

The study builds on earlier work from the Deep History of Sea Country project, which reported similar findings in 2020 and 2023. Researchers believe further investigations could uncover more sites, offering insights into prehistoric settlement, resource movement, and how ancient communities adapted to changing environments. The scale of Australia’s submerged cultural heritage is only beginning to be understood.
doesnt_show: The discovery does not show the exact age of the stone artefacts or whether they were used before or after the landscape was flooded. It also does not reveal the specific activities carried out at the spring or hilltop sites.
settle: Direct dating of the artefacts using methods like optically stimulated luminescence or radiocarbon on associated organic remains would settle their age.
